However, the challenge of producing reliable movements small enough to fit into the diminutive cases required for a ring meant that few examples were made before the 19th century. After a long and successful tenure at the helm of Patek Philippe, an aging Philippe Stern decided that it was time for a natural succession. He gave his son Thierry full creative freedom on the direction of the next perpetual calendar chronograph, a landmark complication in the field of watches and pioneered by none other than Patek Philippe themselves. It was an unofficial test for the young Thierry Stern, and the success of the watch would see him properly inducted into a leadership role. The product of his considerations was a larger watch, but with all the elegance expected of the brand, and with a plethora of design elements taken from the pages of history to appeal to the emotions of Patek Philippe enthusiasts. The 5970 was the largest perpetual calendar chronograph ever produced by Patek Philippe at that point in time, much larger than the previous 3970 which measured 36mm in diameter. Despite the change in size both watches were powered by the base chronograph calibre by Lemania, the 2310, though heavily modified. To ensure that the subsidiary dials did not look Ã¢ÂÂmaroonedÃ¢ÂÂ in the middle of the much larger dial, a tachymeter was added beyond the railroad seconds track, not only to fill up the dial but also as a callback to the first and second series 2499 dials. The square pushers of the 1518 and first series 2499 were also brought back. It can be said that the watch is a perfect combination of vintage callbacks and modern design elements. The reference 5970 stands as a stalwart of collectible, rare and complicated Patek Philippe watches, and despite its relatively young age has already become one of the biggest hits of our millennia.

Cartier, Paris New York retailed A very fine and exceptionally rare yellow gold oval form skeletonised wristwatch, Circa 1973 Dial: skeletonised, blued steel baton hands Calibre: 9Ã¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂ calibre 969 movement signed Cartier Paris, skeletonised bridges with damascened CÃÂ´tes de GenÃÂ¨ve decoration, lever escapement, 18 jewels, annular balance, adjusted to temperature and 3 positions, Breguet balance spring Movement number: 62'840 Case: 18k yellow gold, broad polished bezel with incised Roman and disc-form hour indexes filled with black enamel, satin finishes case sides, sapphire crystals to front and back, beaded cabochon sapphire-set crown, concealed lugs, sapphire crystal case back with broad gold rim secured by four gold screws, outside case back with French eagleÃ¢ÂÂs head assay mark Case number: Cartier stamp with New York Subsidiary stock number 028'141, numbered between lugs beneath case top at 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock with Cartier Paris Reference No. 57'375 and above 12 oÃ¢ÂÂclock 5 Closure: black unsigned leather strap and 18k gold deployant buckle with French assay marks and numbered 25'567, 67 Size: 37.5 mm length x 29 mm width Signed: case, dial and movement Accessories: none Made in circa 1973, this watch dates to a period when traditional watchmaking was increasingly under threat from the advance of the quartz wristwatch. Emphasizing the superior craftsmanship of the fine mechanical watch, the skeletonised movement defiantly separated haute horlogerie from the soulless electrical circuitry of the quartz watch. By placing the movement centre stage, rather than hidden behind a watchÃ¢ÂÂs dial and case back, the mesmerizing intricacy of its mechanics could be fully appreciated. Here the movement plates have been finely cut and shaped to remove as much material as possible, allowing a detailed view of the movementÃ¢ÂÂs mechanics. Exceptionally skilled work, removing so large an area of the movement plates without careful planning and extreme precision would compromise the inherent strength and integrity of the movement itself. Few skeletonised watches manage to so thoroughly reveal a movementÃ¢ÂÂs inner workings. Here not only can the action of the going train, the escapement and the gearing for the hands be clearly observed, but one can also see the action of the hand-setting mechanism and even the coils of the mainspring and its changing condition as it is wound. The movement can be attributed to Audemars Piguet and their TS calibre. It was during the 1930s that Audemars Piguet perfected their skeletonised movement, illuminating it from either side by pierced the plates and bridges from front to back. Executed by their finest watchmakers, who were specially trained for the task, Audemars Piguet created a calibre that was imbued with a unique sense of lightness and transparency. With its smooth pebble-like form, the gold case of this watch has a particularly pleasing geomorphic shape. The bezel is broad with incised hour markers. Cartier engraved bezels with hour indexes for decorative reasons in the Art Deco period, yet here it becomes an essential part of the design, as the only available area on which calibrations for time can be shown. A captivating model, the watch effortlessly combines elements of the Art Deco with traditional watchmaking, while simultaneously creating a thoroughly modern 1970s aesthetic.

description_block: PROPERTY OF AN IMPORTANT ASIAN COLLECTOR Rolex Cosmograph Daytona 'Paul Newman John Player Special Cherry', Reference 6264 A yellow gold chronograph wristwatch with bracelet, Circa 1971 Dial: black, exotic Calibre: cal. 727 mechanical, 17 jewels Case: 14k yellow gold, screw down case back Case number: 2Ã¢ÂÂ802Ã¢ÂÂ702 Closure: 14k yellow gold Rolex Oyster bracelet and folding clasp Size: 37 mm diameter, bracelet circumference approximately 190 mm Signed: case, dial and movement Accessories: none In the Rolex collecting world, several key terms will instantly get any connoisseursÃ¢ÂÂ attention. Daytona. Paul Newman. John Player Special. All of these terms are no stranger to the community, nor to the gavel. Indeed, Paul Newman Daytonas have made up the bulk of high-flying Rolex auction lots in recent years, with John Player Special versions flying higher still. However, this was not the case half a century ago when the Daytona was first introduced. As the well known story goes, the original Daytonas were so unpopular that they would sit in retailer shop windows for years without attracting any interested buyers. This was one of the reasons why, a few years after the release of the reference 6239, Rolex began producing a new dial type in order to add variety and hopefully increase appeal in its struggling chronograph model. Their plan failed, but only for the time being. No one knew it at the time, but Rolex had just created their most desirable dial design, ever. Few manually wound Daytonas were ever made due to their unpopularity at the time, even fewer with exotic dials, and fewer still were cased in gold. Some experts go so far as to estimate that for every Daytona that was cased in gold, ten were cased in stainless steel, with the total amount of gold Daytonas fitted with exotic dials of any colour never exceeding 100 units. It wasnÃ¢ÂÂt until Paul Newman, star of both race track and silver screen was seen wearing an exotic dial 6239 that people began to take notice. The rest, as they say, is history. Yellow gold Paul Newman dials come in three categories: Champagne, Lemon, and the present John Player Special, which signified a black dial with gold accents, aptly named after the iconic Lotus Formula One team which shared the same colour scheme. Champagne examples are the most common, while JPS and Lemon variants are considerably scarcer. Indeed, no more than 20 JPS examples have appeared at auction in the past decade. However, an even scarcer sub-genre of the John Player Special that may be less familiar to the collecting zeitgeist, and indeed has never yet appeared at auction, is the John Player Special Ã¢ÂÂCherryÃ¢ÂÂ. Every single John Player Special dial that has appeared at auction features a gold coloured Ã¢ÂÂDaytonaÃ¢ÂÂ logo above the 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock register, with the majority of these belonging to the reference 6241 and serial numbers scattered roughly around the year 1970. However, another small batch of John Player Special dials have surfaced in 6264 cases with serials clustered in 1971. These dials feature a slightly different gold colour tone, deeper and richer compared to standard John Player Specials, prompting some experts to refer to them as Ã¢ÂÂReverse LemonÃ¢ÂÂ dials. Most importantly, these dials all feature Ã¢ÂÂDaytonaÃ¢ÂÂ Logo in bright red, earning them the moniker Ã¢ÂÂCherryÃ¢ÂÂ. Believed to have been produced as a final batch of gold Paul Newman dials, the handful of known examples are found within a narrow grouping of case numbers. Rarely seen publicly, the JPS cherry has only occasionally featured in reference books and online archives. Further research shows that some 20+ years ago a small group of early vintage Rolex collectors were afforded a tour of the Singer factory, and images from that trip included an example of the JPS cherry within Singers own archives.

PROPERTY OF AN IMPORTANT COLLECTOR Philippe Dufour Simplicity, Number 31 A platinum wristwatch, Circa 2003 Dial: white Calibre: cal. 11 mechanical, 21 jewels Movement number: 31 Case: platinum, snap on sapphire crystal display back Closure: black Philippe Dufour alligator strap and 18k white gold buckle Size: 37 mm diameter Signed: case, dial and movement Accessories: none A legend in watchmaking was born in 1948 in Le Sentier, the VallÃÂ©e de Joux. Instead of pursuing academics, he chose the path of watchmaking and graduated from the Ecole dÃ¢ÂÂHorlogerie de la VallÃÂ©e de Joux. He began his career at prestigious watch brands such as Jaeger-Lecoultre and Audemars Piguet, but had a bigger vision in mind. In 1992, Philippe Dufour shocked the world with his Grande Sonnerie - one of the most challenging watchmaking complications to make and the first of the type to ever be cased in wristwatch form. While it may appear minimalistic, this timepiece is renowned for its exceptional quality with each component hand-finished to perfection by Dufour himself - one watchmaker, start to finish. The watch exemplifies Philippe DufourÃ¢ÂÂs attention to detail and dedication to traditional watchmaking. The entire watch, from the bridges to the screws to the movement and to the case, was handmade using the most traditional watchmaking tools. Cartier, London The Jerry Lee Lewis Ã¢ÂÂBubbleÃ¢ÂÂ A rare and unusual asymmetrically domed yellow gold bubble-form wristwatch, formerly the property of American comedian and actor Jerry Lewis, Circa 1955-56 Dial: silvered dial signed Cartier, black Arabic and baton hour indexes, blued steel ÃÂ©pÃÂ©e hands Calibre: 5ÃÂ¼Ã¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂ rear-wound movement signed Cartier, grained decoration, lever escapement, 16 jewels, annular balance with timing screws Movement number: 503'173 Case: 18k yellow gold domed asymmetrical case, rounded moulded bezel, flat notched winder to case back, case secured by two screws to back, inside case back with London hallmarks for 18k gold, date letter Ã¢ÂÂUÃ¢ÂÂ for 1955-56 and [JC] Jean-Jacques Cartier punch mark Case number: London Stock No. Ã¢ÂÂ¢ 8073 Ã¢ÂÂ¢ Closure: black unsigned leather strap and 18k gold deployant buckle stamped B1933 and London hallmarks for 18ct gold, date letter Ã¢ÂÂNÃ¢ÂÂ for 1968-69 Size: 20 mm diameter Accessories: Cartier presentation box and travelling pouch Jerry Lewis was one of the most influential comedians of the 20th century, known for his electrifying stage presence, exaggerated physical comedy, and inventive approach to filmmaking. Rising to fame in the 1940s as part of the legendary duo Martin & Lewis, he captivated audiences with his manic energy and contrast to Dean MartinÃ¢ÂÂs smooth persona. After their split in 1956, Lewis forged a solo career that redefined Hollywood comedy, both as a performer and director. Films such as The Bellboy (1960), The Ladies Man (1961), and The Nutty Professor (1963) showcased his mastery of slapstick humour while also pushing cinematic boundaries. He pioneered the use of video assist technology, allowing directors to review scenes in real time Ã¢ÂÂ a breakthrough that remains an industry standard today. His influence on comedy spans generations, inspiring artists from Jim Carrey to Martin Scorsese with his fearless, innovative approach. Beyond entertainment, Lewis was also a dedicated humanitarian. As the longtime host of the Muscular Dystrophy AssociationÃ¢ÂÂs Labor Day Telethon, he helped raise over $2.5 billion for medical research, earning him the nickname Ã¢ÂÂThe King of Telethons.Ã¢ÂÂ A collector of fine watches, with a particular preference for smaller-sized models, Lewis owned and wore several different Cartier timepieces, including ladiesÃ¢ÂÂ models, but few were as strikingly unconventional as his bubble-form Cartier from 1955. Quite apart from its extraordinary design, this watch is of great significance due to its period of production. Although Cartier London was already under the leadership of Jean-Jacques Cartier, this predates the 1966Ã¢ÂÂ74 period more frequently associated with the branchÃ¢ÂÂs most avant-garde designs. With its bold, convex form, the watch reflected LewisÃ¢ÂÂs exuberant on-screen persona Ã¢ÂÂ playful, exaggerated, and full of energy. Just as his physical comedy relied on distortion and unpredictability, the watchÃ¢ÂÂs asymmetrically domed shape broke away from traditional watchmaking conventions, embodying a lighthearted yet avant-garde spirit. Beyond aesthetics, it also resonated with LewisÃ¢ÂÂs fascination with technology and innovation. As a pioneer in filmmaking techniques, he consistently embraced new ways to push boundaries, much like the bubble form in mid-century design symbolised modernity and futurism. The watchÃ¢ÂÂs production era coincided with the height of 1950s space-age optimism, mirroring LewisÃ¢ÂÂs own rise to stardom during HollywoodÃ¢ÂÂs golden era. As an entertainer who thrived on reinvention and spectacle, it seems only fitting that Lewis would wear a timepiece that so effortlessly captured the essence of his showmanship and singular vision. The 1950s were a decade captivated by progress, technology, and the dream of the future, and the bubble form became a defining aesthetic across fashion, industrial design, and futuristic innovation. This rare Cartier London model epitomises this cultural movement, embodying the eraÃ¢ÂÂs fascination with fluid, organic shapes and a vision of modernity that felt both playful and sophisticated. During this period, fashion designers such as Christian Dior and Pierre Balmain experimented with rounded, sculptural silhouettes, while futuristic couturiers like Pierre Cardin and AndrÃÂ© CourrÃÂ¨ges later embraced bubble-inspired designs that evoked space helmets and domed enclosures. Accessories echoed this aesthetic, with womenÃ¢ÂÂs sunglasses, handbags, and jewellery adopting curved, convex forms that suggested a streamlined, ultra-modern elegance. Beyond fashion, the 1950s were defined by an obsession with space exploration, aerodynamics, and the promise of new materials. The success of early rocketry and the dawning of the space age inspired industrial designers to incorporate spherical, domed, and capsule like structures into everything from automobiles to architecture. Bubble cars, such as the BMW Isetta and Messerschmitt KR200, became symbols of efficiency and forward-thinking design, while televisions, radios, and clocks featured convex, domed glass to emphasise their modernity. More than just an accessory, LewisÃ¢ÂÂs Cartier bubble watch embodied this spirit of progress Ã¢ÂÂ a timepiece that captured the eraÃ¢ÂÂs optimism, innovation, and boundless imagination. It was a watch for a new world, where humour, artistry, and the thrill of the future converged in a single, sculptural form.

Cartier, London Montre bracelet Curviligne dans Anneaux Ovale An extremely rare and unusual yellow gold oval wristwatch within a larger oval frame with teardrop t-bar lugs and original gold deployant buckle with the clasp of matching design, Circa 1971-72 Dial: silvered dial with incised Cartier signature, blued steel ÃÂ©pÃÂ©e hands Calibre: 6ÃÂ½Ã¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂ oval calibre 845 movement signed LeCoultre Co., grained decoration, lever escapement, 17 jewels, annular balance, unadjusted, flat hairspring, Incabloc shock absorber Movement number: maniplate numbered 2'079'125 Case: 18k yellow gold oval case set within outer gold ring with teardrop lugs with pink gold t-bars, case back secured by four screws to case sides, beaded cabochon sapphire-set crown Case number: inside case back with London hallmarks for 18k gold, date letter Ã¢ÂÂqÃ¢ÂÂ for 1971-72, [JC] Jean-Jacques Cartier punch mark and numbered 9'916 Closure: black unsigned leather strap and 18k yellow and pink gold deployant buckle, the clasp of double semi oval form, London hallmarks for 18k gold, date letter Ã¢ÂÂqÃ¢ÂÂ for 1971-72, [JC] Jean-Jacques Cartier punch mark and numbered 9'916 Size: 46 mm length x 37 mm width Accessories: none At the time of this watchÃ¢ÂÂs production, Cartier London was at the height of its most experimental and creative period, producing some of the brandÃ¢ÂÂs boldest, most unconventional wristwatches. Unlike Cartier Paris, which remained rooted in tradition, Cartier London pursued a distinctly avant-garde approach, reinterpreting heritage models while pushing the boundaries of form, proportion, and openness in design. This watch embodies that same philosophy, featuring a floating horizontal oval dial set within a larger vertical oval frame, creating a dynamic interplay of geometry and balance. The concept of placing one form within another has precedents in earlier Cartier designs, particularly those that combined square or round cases within oval or circular outer frames. In this 1971 Cartier London creation, the relationship between two interlocking ovals is further refined, transforming the watch into an object of fluidity and sculptural elegance. The dial appears to float, its clean, numeral-free surface reinforcing the purity of the design. Unusually, it is subtly incised with the script-form Cartier signature, adding a discreet yet refined detail. The outer oval frame is interrupted only by two teardrop-shaped gold motifs at 12 and 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock, which, in addition to serving as decorative highlights, have a structural purpose Ã¢ÂÂ concealing the lug bars that secure the strap. This formation not only introduces a focal point but also advances Cartier LondonÃ¢ÂÂs signature design ethos of the era, in which watch cases were crafted to create the illusion of floating seamlessly above their straps. Here, however, that concept is pushed even further Ã¢ÂÂ a void is deliberately introduced beneath the case, resulting in a striking suspension effect that isolates the watch entirely from its strap. The composition is defined by two interlocking ovals, with both the central case and the surrounding frame adopting elongated oval forms. This creates a layered sense of depth, reinforcing the floating effect while adding a dynamic interplay of curves. The central oval case also gives the impression that it could rotate within the outer frame, adding a further sense of movement and playfulness to the design. Beyond its structural ingenuity, the watchÃ¢ÂÂs overall composition also evokes an abstracted interpretation of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs back-to-back double C logo. The interplay between the two oval forms mirrors the fluid, interlocking curves of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs monogram, subtly incorporating an element of brand heritage into an avant-garde, sculptural form. The teardrop-shaped gold motifs at 12 and 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock further enhance this visual connection, recalling the way the Cartier emblemÃ¢ÂÂs mirrored Cs interweave to create balance and symmetry. Given Cartier LondonÃ¢ÂÂs experimental approach during this period, it is entirely possible that this design was conceived as a reinterpretation of the MaisonÃ¢ÂÂs signature motif, transforming it into a wearable expression of the brandÃ¢ÂÂs identity through shape and proportion rather than literal branding. This model is also exceptionally rare Ã¢ÂÂ to date, our research has not found any other examples, further adding to its allure. While it is uncertain whether this was a special order, the level of innovation, sculptural presence, and the apparent rarity of this example suggest that it may have been a bespoke commission or an experimental creation. It was through Jean-Jacques CartierÃ¢ÂÂs close collaboration with his chief designer, Rupert Emmerson, that innovative designs such as this became possible, ultimately executed by hand in the Cartier London-run Wright & Davies workshops.

The exaggerated elongation of the Roman numerals at 12 and 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock further reinforces this approach, a graphic flourish that adds dynamism and energy to the design. To mark the occasion, Journe coated both the dial and movement in Ruthenium, giving this series an instantly recognisable and sleek aesthetic. To possess any Journe is special, but the Ruthenium Tourbillon stands as a significant and rare edition of the model line most dear to the man himself.
